figures.caption: Figure 1 – Individual monotony avoidance in humans reflects boredom and is driven by low information content: (a) Modified 127 two-alternative forced choice task to assess human choice behavior between a monotonous alternative – a button (btn) providing 128 repetitive stimuli – and a variable alternative – a button providing diverse stimuli (mon-var)22. Participants also completed control 129 conditions with equivalent stimulation of both alternatives (mon-mon, var-var). Visual analog scale (VAS) ratings of current 130 sentiment were collected intermittently. Table depicts stimulus library sizes for various conditions. (b) Mean preference over time 131 across conditions (n=92 participants throughout). Arrowheads indicate ratings; data are mean ± SEM. (c) Distribution of mean 132 preference during the second half of each condition (gray shading in b). Black bars, mean ± SEM; ***: p<0.001, n.s.: p>0.05. (d) 133 State boredom before and after the choice task, assessed with the Multidimensional State Boredom Scale (MSBS). ***: p<0.001. 134 (e) Correlation of mean perceived boredom and monotony avoidance (preference for the variable alternative) in the mon-var 135 condition. Black line, linear fit; shading, 95% confidence interval. (f) Boredom ratings increased over the mon-var condition in 136 parallel with monotony avoidance. Data are mean ± SEM; ***: p<0.001. (g) Affect and arousal ratings across the mon-var 137 condition, indicating increasing displeasure and decreasing arousal over time. Data are mean ± SEM; ***: p<0.001. (h) Schematic 138 of empirical entropy as a trial-wise measure of experienced information content (Methods). (i) Mean experienced entropy for the 139 monotonous and variable alternatives over time in the mon-var condition. Data are mean ± SEM; ***: p<0.001. (j) Choice 140 probability in the task as a function of difference in previously experienced entropy between both alternatives. To compute the 141 choice probabilities, the single-trial data was binned according to experienced entropy difference (Methods). Gray lines, individual 142 participants; pink line and shading, mean ± SEM. (k) Logistic regression model incorporating sensitivity to experienced entropy 143 differences, idiosyncratic choice bias and a tendency to repeat the previous choice (left), and individual prediction performance 144

Figure 2 – Mice exhibit analogous monotony avoidance driven by low information content: (a) Translational mouse version of 216 the choice task between monotonous and variable auditory stimulation. Mice were tracked in Skinner box with two mirror-image 217 zones and presented with different types of auditory stimuli depending on their current location (left). In addition to the 218 comparison of monotony and variability (mon-var) and equivalent stimulation (mon-mon, var-var), mice underwent various 219 control conditions including no stimulation (sil: silence) or loud white noise (noise) (right). Table depicts library sizes and stimulus 220 types for various conditions. (b) Movement trajectory of one example mouse in a session of the mon-var task. (c) Mean movement 221 over time in the mon-var condition (n=24 mice throughout), showing progressive settling within one zone. Data are mean ± SEM. 222 (d,e) Mean place preference over time in the mon-var (d) and silence (e) conditions. Mice avoided monotonous stimulation but 223 showed no bias between silent zones. Data are mean ± SEM. (f) Mean spatial occupancy across mice and sessions for all conditions. 224 (g) Mean place preference during the second half of each condition (shading in d,e), showing preference for less monotonous 225 stimulation and avoidance of loud white noise. Black bars, mean ± SEM. (h) Mean experienced empirical entropy for the 226 monotonous and variable zones over time in the mon-var condition (Methods; Figure 1h,i). Data are mean ± SEM.; ***: p<0.001. 227 (i) Choice probability as a function of the difference in previously experienced entropy between zones. Data were binned by 228 entropy difference (Methods). Gray lines, individual mice; pink line and shading, mean ± SEM. (j) Logistic regression model 229 incorporating sensitivity to experienced entropy differences, idiosyncratic choice bias and choice repetition (left), and prediction 230 performance for mouse location (right; >90% correct; ***: p<0.001). (k) Contributions of model parameters to choice behavior, 231 showing a dominant contribution of entropy, consistent with the human results (see Figure 1l). *: p<0.05, **: p<0.01, ***: p<0.001. 232

Figure 3 – Sensory information content is reflected by the magnitude of evoked cortical activity in humans and mice: (a) Ten 272 sounds (spectrogram range, 16 Hz–15 kHz, 0.5s) were used to generate 20 entropy-varying sequences of ten sounds, each 273 presented in three stimulus versions (60 sequences total). Participants either rated the sequences (n=92) or underwent 64-274 channel EEG and pupillometry during passive listening (n=12). (b) After each sequence, participants rated perceived boredom, 275 information content, pleasantness (affect) and arousal. (c) Ratings for the five highest- and five lowest-entropy sequences (n=92). 276 Box plots show median and interquartile range; vertical bars, mean ± SEM; *: p<0.05, n.s.: p>0.05. (d) Mean EEG responses across 277 Fz and Cz (left) and pupil responses (right) to example high- and low-entropy sequences. Inset, mean sound-evoked potentials 278 across all sounds in each sequence, showing a larger P200 for the high-entropy sequence (see Supplementary Figure 5b,c; EEG 279 responses are from n=12 participants; pupil responses are from n=8 participants). Data are mean ± SEM; dark and light traces 280 indicate high- and low-entropy sequences, respectively; gray shading indicates stimulus presentation and dashed lines baseline. 281 (e) Correlations of mean entropy and mean evoked P200 amplitude (left), or pupil dilatation (right) across 20 sequences, averaged 282 across stimulus versions and participants. Gray lines show linear fits; error bars, SEM. (f) Standardized coefficients from a linear 283 regression relating P200 and pupil responses to mean sequence entropy. Error bars, 95% confidence intervals. n.s.: p>0.05, **: 284

Figure 4 – A representational code of information content driven by neurons tuned to stimulus entropy: (a) Example FOV from 354 two-photon calcium imaging, showing broad GCaMP6m and H2B::mCherry expression in cortical layer 2/3 neurons. Scale bar: 355 50μm. (b) Calcium responses (ΔF/F0) to sound sequences with varying entropy of example neurons. (c) Mean ΔF/F0 responses to 356 six example sounds (rows) for three example neurons (displayed as mean ± SEM). Figure 5 –Network mechanisms enabling the representation of information content: (a) Experimental signatures the model aims 503 to reproduce. Left: trial-averaged population response across a low-entropy (fully repetitive) and a high-entropy (fully variable) 504 sound sequence. Center, right: PCA projection of the representational map, colored by stimulus identity (equivalent to Figure 4l 505 and Supplementary Figure 7d). Marker size depicts entropy bins (center) or mean response magnitude bins (right). (b) Schematic 506 of the recurrent network model with distinct mechanisms for afferent synaptic plasticity and recurrent synaptic plasticity.
